statement: If $3 \le 2x - 5 < 11$, what is the greatest possible integer value of $4x - 3$?

choices.misconception: I added 5 only to the left part, getting $8 \le 2x < 11$, so $4x - 3 < 19$ and I picked 18.
I found $13 \le 4x - 3 < 29$ but included 29, even though the upper inequality is strict.
I took the greatest integer value of $x$, which is 7, and computed $4(7) - 3$, but $x$ does not have to be an integer.

hints: Solve the compound inequality for $x$ first.
Add $5$ to all three parts and divide by $2$. Then build $4x - 3$ from the bounds on $x$, remembering that $x$ need not be a whole number.
$4 \le x < 8$, so $13 \le 4x - 3 < 29$. Find the greatest integer in that range.

solutions.reliable: Add $5$ to every part: $8 \le 2x < 16$. Divide by $2$: $4 \le x < 8$. Multiply by $4$ and subtract $3$: $13 \le 4x - 3 < 29$. The expression can take any value in this range, including $28$ (when $x = 7.75$), but not $29$. So the greatest integer value is $28$. Key idea: transform a compound inequality into the expression you need, and notice which quantity is required to be an integer.
solutions.elegant: Since $4x - 3 = 2(2x - 5) + 7$, doubling $3 \le 2x - 5 < 11$ and adding $7$ gives $13 \le 4x - 3 < 29$ at once.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
